lesson.title: Stem and Leaf: Keeping Every Digit in Sight
lesson.summary: A stemplot splits each numeric value into a stem and a leaf so it can display the distribution of a quantitative variable while still preserving every original digit.
lesson.body:
A stemplot, also called a stem and leaf plot, is another way to display the distribution of a quantitative variable, and like a dotplot, it preserves every individual data value rather than grouping them away. Each numeric value is split into two parts: a stem, made of the leading digit or digits, and a leaf, made of the final digit. The stems are listed once in a column from smallest to largest, and every data value contributes one leaf digit written next to its matching stem.

To build a stemplot, first decide where to split each value into stem and leaf, typically using all but the last digit as the stem for two digit numbers. Then list every possible stem once in order down the left side of the plot, and for each data value, write its leaf digit in a row next to the correct stem, keeping the leaves within each row in increasing order for readability. Unlike a dotplot's dots or a bar's height, a stemplot literally spells out the last digit of every value, so no numeric precision is lost.

Consider 12 test scores: 62, 67, 71, 73, 74, 78, 81, 85, 85, 89, 92, 95. Using the tens digit as the stem and the ones digit as the leaf, the stemplot has four stems, 6, 7, 8, and 9. Stem 6 has leaves 2 and 7, representing 62 and 67. Stem 7 has leaves 1, 3, 4, and 8, representing 71, 73, 74, and 78. Stem 8 has leaves 1, 5, 5, and 9, representing 81, 85, 85, and 89. Stem 9 has leaves 2 and 5, representing 92 and 95. Counting leaves confirms nothing was lost: 2 plus 4 plus 4 plus 2 equals 12, matching all 12 original scores.

A key with the stemplot, such as noting that stem 6, leaf 2 means 62, removes any ambiguity about where the decimal or place value falls, which matters because the same digits could represent very different numbers depending on the variable being measured. Reading this stemplot sideways, rotating it 90 degrees in your mind, produces essentially the same shape a histogram would show for this data, with more values piling up in the 70s and 80s and fewer at the extremes in the 60s and 90s.

Stemplots have two features that make them especially useful teaching and exploration tools. A back to back stemplot shares one column of stems in the middle with leaves for two different groups extending to the left and right, making it easy to compare two distributions directly, such as test scores for two different class periods. A split stem, where each stem digit is used twice to hold a narrower range of leaves, such as leaves 0 through 4 on one line and 5 through 9 on the next, gives finer detail for data that clusters heavily around just a few stems, a preview of the trade offs involved in choosing bin width for a histogram.

Stemplots also handle data with three or more digits by simply adjusting which digits become the stem and which single digit becomes the leaf, though only one final digit is ever used as a leaf, with any digits beyond that typically truncated or rounded so the plot stays readable. This flexibility, combined with the fact that a stemplot can be built quickly by hand from nothing more than sorted data, is part of why it remains a standard first look at a small or moderate sized quantitative data set before moving to a histogram.
